title: How to Actually Work Smarter
author: Ethan Evans
source: Level Up with Ethan Evans (Substack), August 6, 2026
summary: Ethan Evans's Level Up newsletter argues that chronically overworked ICs and managers don't have an effort problem — they have a selection problem, spreading full effort across too many tasks instead of deciding what deserves more, less, or no effort at all. He contends that working harder is often a way of postponing the uncomfortable decisions that working smarter requires, since choosing priorities means risking being wrong. The core technique he offers is replacing 'What am I supposed to do?' with 'What outcome are we trying to create?' and 'What decision will this work help us make?' — questions designed to reveal whether the requested deliverable actually is the goal, or just one path to it. The piece closes by insisting working smarter is a trainable skill, not a fixed trait.
points: Reframes chronic overwork as a prioritization/selection problem rather than an effort or personality problem.
Argues working harder often functions as a way to avoid the harder task of choosing priorities and risking being wrong.
Recommends replacing 'What am I supposed to do?' with 'What outcome are we trying to create?' to surface better options.
Frames risk-taking as the necessary cost of good judgment.
Positions 'working smarter' as a learnable, practical skill rather than an innate trait.
quotes: Overworked people do not have an effort problem. They have a selection problem.
They are working hard on too many things because they have not decided which work deserves more effort, less effort, or none at all.
The reason so many people simply work harder (instead of smarter) is that working harder postpones difficult decisions.
Risk is the cost of good judgment. The alternative is trying to do everything equally, without judgment.
When you understand the objective behind a task, you discover a better way to achieve it.
Finding a better way to get the business what they want is the epitome of working smarter, not harder.
The good news is that working smarter is not a personality trait. It is a skill.
